# Acquisition Research

**Paid visitors bounce off landing pages**

> I clicked the ad expecting one thing, the page doesn't match it, so I leave.

How might we make the landing page deliver on the promise the ad made?

## You'll recognise this when

- High ad spend with weak ROAS

- High landing-page bounce

- Poor message match between the ad and the page

## What this recipe does

Paid traffic is arriving but converting poorly, and it is unclear whether the problem sits in the ads, the landing pages, or the match between the two. This recipe connects acquisition spend to the on-site experience so you can improve ROAS rather than simply cut budget.
Ads analysis and analytics data analysis set the quantitative picture: which campaigns and channels underperform, and what those visitors do once they land. A UX heuristic review flags likely friction on the landing pages, and a 5 second test reveals whether the first impression and message match the promise made in the ad. The data shows where the leak is, the qualitative methods suggest why, and optimisation effort lands on the right page with the right message.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Set the quantitative picture: which campaigns underperform, and what those visitors do once they land.

- [Ads Analysis](/research-methods/ads-analysis)

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

### Focus
Flag likely friction on the landing pages themselves.

- [UX Heuristic Review](/research-methods/ux-heuristic-review)

### Validate
Check the first impression matches the promise the ad made.

- [5 Second Test](/research-methods/five-second-test)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/acquisition-research
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# B2B ICP Research

**We don't really understand our ICP**

> Nothing on the site convinces me it's built for a company like mine.

How might we speak to our ICP's real motivations, triggers and doubts?

## You'll recognise this when

- Messaging built on internal assumptions

- Unclear persona definition

- Weak win rates against competitors

## What this recipe does

Messaging and targeting are running on assumptions about who the ideal customer is and what drives them. This recipe builds a grounded picture of the ICP: their motivations, triggers, and fears, uncertainties and doubts. The picture starts in the CRM record, where win-loss analysis shows who actually buys and who walks. The interviews go deep, the polls add immediacy and scale, and the usability sessions tie attitude to behaviour. The messaging built on all of it then gets tested with the people it describes before it ships.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Get the real language and hesitations behind a decision to buy, from the CRM record and the buyers themselves.

- [Customer Interviews](/research-methods/customer-interviews)

- [Win-loss Analysis (CRM Analysis)](/research-methods/win-loss-analysis)

- [Win-loss Interviews](/research-methods/win-loss-interviews)

### Focus
Capture intent and barriers from people evaluating you right now, and tie attitude to behaviour.

- [On-site Polls](/research-methods/on-site-polls)

- [Remote Usability Studies](/research-methods/remote-usability-studies)

### Validate
Test the messaging built on it with the people it describes before it ships.

- [Copy Testing](/research-methods/copy-testing)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/b2b-icp-research
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Brand Perception Baseline & Tracking

**We don't know how the market sees us**

> I've heard the name, but I couldn't tell you what they do differently or whether they're for someone like me.

How might we know how our market actually perceives us, and whether that perception is moving?

## You'll recognise this when

- A rebrand or repositioning is being scoped with no baseline of current awareness or perception

- Positioning debates inside the company run on opinion because nobody has market evidence

- Sales keeps correcting the same wrong assumptions about what the company does

- The brand is missing from consideration sets it should be in

## What this recipe does

A rebrand, relaunch or repositioning is coming, and nobody can say how the market sees the brand today, which means nobody will be able to say whether the work changed anything. This recipe builds the baseline first so the after has a before.
The explore work reads what the market says unprompted. Social listening and review analysis surface the words people already use about the brand and its competitors, branded search demand shows how many go looking by name, and sales and support know which wrong assumptions keep recurring. A panel survey of the target market, rather than the customer list, then quantifies unaided and aided awareness, preference and perception against named competitors, while copy testing checks whether the intended positioning lands with the people it describes. Validation is longitudinal rather than a one-off check. The same survey, run against the same profile after the change, turns before and after from a feeling into a measurement.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Read what the market says unprompted: conversations, reviews, and demand for the brand by name.

- [Social Media Listening](/research-methods/social-media-listening)

- [Online Review Analysis](/research-methods/online-review-analysis)

- [Search & SERP Analysis](/research-methods/search-serp-analysis)

- [Sales / Customer Service Interviews](/research-methods/sales-customer-service-interviews)

### Focus
Quantify awareness, preference and perception against named competitors, and check the positioning language lands.

- [Brand Perception Survey](/research-methods/brand-perception-survey)

- [Copy Testing](/research-methods/copy-testing)

### Validate
Re-run the same measurement after the change and compare to the baseline.

- [Brand Perception Survey](/research-methods/brand-perception-survey)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/brand-perception-tracking
Last updated: 2026-08-06

# Category & Listing Page Optimisation

**Shoppers browse categories but don't click into products**

> I'm scrolling the category page but nothing helps me narrow it down, so I leave without picking anything.

How might we help shoppers narrow the range and find a product worth clicking?

## You'll recognise this when

- High category-page exits

- Low listing-to-product click-through

- Filters and sorting applied then abandoned

- Deep scrolling with few product clicks

## What this recipe does

Shoppers reach the category and listing pages but leave without clicking into a product, and it is unclear whether the range, the filters or the product cards are to blame. Analytics sizes the problem first, showing which categories leak the most and how listing visits relate to product views. Heatmaps and session recordings then reveal how people actually work the page: what they filter and sort, how far they scroll, and which product cards earn attention. An on-site poll asks browsers what is stopping them narrowing down. Usability sessions validate a revised listing experience against real find-and-choose tasks, so changes to filters, sorting and card content follow the way shoppers genuinely shop the range.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Size the problem: which categories leak most, and how listing visits relate to product views.

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

### Focus
Watch how people work the page, and ask what's stopping them narrowing down.

- [Heatmaps](/research-methods/heatmaps)

- [Session Recordings](/research-methods/session-recordings)

- [On-site Polls](/research-methods/on-site-polls)

### Validate
Test a revised listing experience against real find-and-choose tasks.

- [Remote Usability Studies](/research-methods/remote-usability-studies)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/category-listing-page
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Checkout & Cart Optimisation

**Shoppers abandon at the payment step**

> I was ready to buy, then the checkout asked for too much or felt unsafe, so I bailed.

How might we get ready-to-buy shoppers through checkout without losing them?

## You'll recognise this when

- High cart abandonment

- Drop-off concentrated on the payment or shipping step

- Repeated 'is this secure' support queries

## What this recipe does

Shoppers add items to the basket and then leave before paying, and the team can't see what tips them out. Start broad to find where value leaks. Analytics shows which checkout steps lose the most people, while session recordings and heatmaps show what those people actually do at the moment they drop. Then focus in on the payment and address fields with form analytics, and ask leavers why with an exit poll. Finish by validating a reworked flow in remote usability sessions before it goes near a build, so several independent signals point at the same fix.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Find which steps lose the most people, and watch what they do at the moment they drop.

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

- [Session Recordings](/research-methods/session-recordings)

- [Heatmaps](/research-methods/heatmaps)

### Focus
Zoom into the payment and address fields, and ask leavers why.

- [Form Analytics](/research-methods/form-analytics)

- [On-site Polls](/research-methods/on-site-polls)

### Validate
Prove the reworked flow with observed tasks and a live test.

- [Remote Usability Studies](/research-methods/remote-usability-studies)

- [A/B Testing](/research-methods/ab-testing)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/checkout-cart-optimisation
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Churn & Retention Research

**We don't know why customers churn**

> I signed up but stopped getting enough value to justify keeping the subscription.

How might we understand and reduce the reasons customers leave?

## You'll recognise this when

- Rising churn

- Low repeat usage

- Cancellation reasons citing value or fit

## What this recipe does

Customers cancel and the business is left guessing whether it was price, value, a missing feature or a bad experience. Start with the traces customers leave behind. Analytics shows where usage tails off before a cancellation, CRM and win-loss data show patterns in who leaves, and live chat logs surface the complaints that recur. A cancellation survey then quantifies the leading reasons, and interviews with churned customers explain the why behind the numbers. The layers turn a vague churn figure into specific, addressable causes.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus.

### Explore
Read the traces customers leave behind: usage, CRM patterns, recurring complaints.

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

- [Win-loss Analysis (CRM Analysis)](/research-methods/win-loss-analysis)

- [Live Chat Analysis](/research-methods/live-chat-analysis)

### Focus
Quantify the leading reasons, then hear the why in customers' own words.

- [Customer Survey](/research-methods/customer-survey)

- [Customer Interviews](/research-methods/customer-interviews)

Where's Validate? For this problem, validation lands in the experimentation programme itself: the hypotheses this research produces become A/B tests and product bets, measured against the outcome metric.

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/churn-retention
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Content-to-Lead Conversion Research

**Organic visitors read the content and leave**

> The article was useful. I read it, got what I needed and left. Nothing made a next step feel worth it.

How might we turn content readers into subscribers and leads without wrecking the reading experience?

## You'll recognise this when

- Content traffic grows steadily while lead volume stays flat

- Strong rankings and high entrances on posts with near-zero CTA engagement

- The newsletter and gated offers barely grow despite real readership

## What this recipe does

The content programme is doing its job of attracting readers, and then the relationship ends at the last paragraph. This recipe finds where the reader-to-lead path breaks. Analytics shows which posts attract visitors with any buying intent and where readers exit, heatmaps show whether the calls to action are even seen on the templates readers actually use, and on-site polls ask readers directly what they came for and what would make a next step worthwhile. Testing offer and CTA framings on a panel, then checking they register at a glance, de-risks the fix before it ships across hundreds of posts.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Find which posts attract buying intent and where readers exit.

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

- [Heatmaps](/research-methods/heatmaps)

### Focus
Ask readers what they came for and what would make a next step worth it.

- [On-site Polls](/research-methods/on-site-polls)

### Validate
Test offer and CTA framings, then check they register at a glance.

- [Copy Testing](/research-methods/copy-testing)

- [5 Second Test](/research-methods/five-second-test)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/content-to-lead
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Conversion Research

**Visitors fail to convert across the site**

> Something keeps stopping me finishing what I came to do, but it's not one obvious thing.

How might we find and remove the biggest on-site barriers to conversion?

## You'll recognise this when

- Below-benchmark conversion rate

- No single clear drop-off

- Need to build a prioritised test pipeline

## What this recipe does

You need a complete view of where and why visitors fail to convert across the site, not just on a single page. This is the broad diagnostic that feeds an experimentation programme.
It deliberately triangulates across data types. Analytics data analysis, heatmaps and session recordings give the quantitative behavioural picture of where users drop off. Customer surveys and on-site polls add the voice of the customer: the motivations, fears and barriers behind that behaviour. Remote usability studies show real people attempting core journeys, and a UX heuristic review provides an expert read to anchor and prioritise. No single method is trusted on its own; the value comes from where the behavioural, attitudinal and observed evidence agree.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Build the quantitative behavioural picture and an expert baseline.

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

- [Heatmaps](/research-methods/heatmaps)

- [Session Recordings](/research-methods/session-recordings)

- [UX Heuristic Review](/research-methods/ux-heuristic-review)

### Focus
Add the voice of the customer behind the behaviour.

- [Customer Survey](/research-methods/customer-survey)

- [On-site Polls](/research-methods/on-site-polls)

### Validate
Watch real people attempt the core journeys.

- [Remote Usability Studies](/research-methods/remote-usability-studies)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/conversion-research
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Engagement Decay & Habit Research

**Activated customers drift away after the early weeks**

> I liked it at first. Then life got busy, I stopped opening it, and nothing gave me a reason to come back.

How might we help the product earn a place in customers' routines after the novelty fades?

## You'll recognise this when

- Activation numbers look healthy while week-four-plus retention slides

- A wide gap between weekly and monthly active customers

- Exit surveys say "just stopped using it" more than any specific complaint

## What this recipe does

These customers activated, found value, and then drifted; not because anything broke, but because the product never earned a place in the routine. Onboarding research won't catch this, because the loss happens after onboarding succeeds. Cohort analysis shows which behaviours separate the customers who stay from the ones who fade and when the fade starts. Diary studies then do what no analytics can: a week or two inside customers' real routines showing where the product fits, what competes with it, and what quietly replaces it. Interviews with drifted-but-recoverable customers explain what changed. Re-engagement and habit-hook concepts get prototype-tested before anything is built.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Find which behaviours separate the customers who stay from the ones who fade, and when the fade starts.

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

### Focus
Spend a week or two inside customers' real routines, then hear what changed from the drifters.

- [Diary Studies](/research-methods/diary-studies)

- [Customer Interviews](/research-methods/customer-interviews)

### Validate
Prototype-test re-engagement and habit hooks before anything is built.

- [Prototype Testing](/research-methods/prototype-testing)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/engagement-decay
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Involuntary Churn & Payment Recovery Research

**Subscriptions end on failed payments, not decisions**

> My card expired and the subscription just stopped. I never decided to leave, and nothing brought me back.

How might we catch and recover the customers who never chose to churn?

## You'll recognise this when

- Churn reporting doesn't split voluntary from involuntary

- A chunk of cancellations show no engagement decline beforehand

- Support keeps fielding "why was I cancelled" and "can't update my card" tickets

## What this recipe does

A meaningful slice of churn is customers who never decided to leave; a payment failed, the retries ran out, and the subscription ended for someone who wanted to keep it. This recipe sizes and explains that leak. Payment funnel analysis shows where charges fail and how many recover, CRM analysis shows who lapses this way and what they were worth, and support logs surface the billing friction customers hit when they try to fix it themselves. A survey of lapsed involuntary customers answers the question the data can't: did they even know, and what would have caught it. Recovery messaging and the update-payment flow get tested before they carry the fix.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Size the leak: where charges fail, how many recover, and what those customers were worth.

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

- [Win-loss Analysis (CRM Analysis)](/research-methods/win-loss-analysis)

### Focus
Surface the billing friction customers hit, and ask lapsed customers whether they even knew.

- [Live Chat Analysis](/research-methods/live-chat-analysis)

- [Customer Survey](/research-methods/customer-survey)

### Validate
Test the recovery messaging and the update-payment flow before they carry the fix.

- [Copy Testing](/research-methods/copy-testing)

- [Prototype Testing](/research-methods/prototype-testing)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/involuntary-churn
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Landing Page Optimisation

**Paid visitors bounce off landing pages**

> I clicked the ad expecting one thing, the page doesn't match it, so I leave.

How might we make the landing page deliver on the promise the ad made?

## You'll recognise this when

- High ad spend with weak ROAS

- High landing-page bounce

- Poor message match between the ad and the page

## What this recipe does

A landing page is underperforming and you need to understand what is blocking visitors before redesigning it. The aim is to diagnose friction across first impression, message and on-page behaviour.
A 5 second test and a UX heuristic review give a fast read on clarity and obvious friction. Heatmaps and session recordings show where attention goes and where people hesitate or drop off. On-site polls ask visitors directly what is missing or unclear, and copy testing checks whether the core message lands with the target audience. The behavioural data shows what is happening, the polls and copy testing explain why, and the heuristic review and 5 second test surface quick wins to act on first.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Get a fast read on clarity and obvious friction.

- [5 Second Test](/research-methods/five-second-test)

- [UX Heuristic Review](/research-methods/ux-heuristic-review)

### Focus
See where attention goes, where people drop, and ask them what's missing.

- [Heatmaps](/research-methods/heatmaps)

- [Session Recordings](/research-methods/session-recordings)

- [On-site Polls](/research-methods/on-site-polls)

- [Copy Testing](/research-methods/copy-testing)

### Validate
Confirm the winning change with a live experiment.

- [A/B Testing](/research-methods/ab-testing)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/landing-page-optimisation

# Lead-Gen Form Optimisation

**Prospects abandon the lead form**

> I started filling in the form but it asked too much or broke, so I stopped.

How might we make the lead form quick and painless enough to finish?

## You'll recognise this when

- Low form completion rate

- Drop-off on specific fields

- High cost per lead from paid traffic

## What this recipe does

Prospects start the lead form but abandon it before submitting, and the cost of every lost completion is high. Form analytics is the spine here, showing the exact fields where people stall, re-enter or quit, and session recordings add the behaviour around those fields. Analytics frames how many are affected, and an on-site poll asks what stopped them. A shortened or restructured form is then checked in usability sessions before launch, so the changes are grounded in where the friction genuinely sits.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Locate the exact fields where people stall, and frame how many are affected.

- [Form Analytics](/research-methods/form-analytics)

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

### Focus
Watch behaviour around those fields, and ask what stopped them.

- [Session Recordings](/research-methods/session-recordings)

- [Heatmaps](/research-methods/heatmaps)

- [On-site Polls](/research-methods/on-site-polls)

### Validate
Check the restructured form in usability sessions before launch.

- [Remote Usability Studies](/research-methods/remote-usability-studies)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/lead-gen-form

# Lead Quality Research

**The pipeline fills with leads sales can't close**

> I downloaded the guide because it looked useful. I was never going to buy anything.

How might we attract fewer, better-fit leads instead of more of the wrong ones?

## You'll recognise this when

- Lead targets get hit while pipeline and revenue stay thin

- Sales rejects, recycles or quietly ignores a large share of handed-over leads

- Gated content fills the CRM with students, researchers and job-seekers

## What this recipe does

The lead count looks healthy and the pipeline doesn't, which usually means the acquisition engine is optimised for volume rather than fit. This recipe diagnoses the gap from both ends. CRM analysis separates the sources, campaigns and offers that produce closed-won customers from the ones that produce noise, and structured input from the whole sales team turns "the leads are junk" into specific, recurring rejection patterns. Interviews with recent well-fit buyers establish what a good lead actually looked like on the way in. Panel testing then checks that requalified messaging and offers attract the buyer and politely lose the browser.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Separate the sources that produce customers from the ones that produce noise, through the CRM and the sales floor.

- [Win-loss Analysis (CRM Analysis)](/research-methods/win-loss-analysis)

- [Sales / Customer Service Interviews](/research-methods/sales-customer-service-interviews)

- [Sales / Customer Service Survey](/research-methods/sales-customer-service-survey)

### Focus
Hear the decision firsthand, from well-fit buyers and the deals that got away.

- [Customer Interviews](/research-methods/customer-interviews)

- [Win-loss Interviews](/research-methods/win-loss-interviews)

### Validate
Check requalified messaging attracts the buyer and politely loses the browser.

- [Copy Testing](/research-methods/copy-testing)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/lead-quality
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Mobile Experience Optimisation

**Mobile converts far worse than desktop**

> On my phone the site is fiddly, so I give up and mean to come back later, but I don't.

How might we close the gap between mobile and desktop conversion?

## You'll recognise this when

- Mobile conversion well below desktop

- High mobile share of traffic

- Mis-tap and zoom behaviour in recordings

## What this recipe does

Mobile traffic is large but converts well below desktop, and the team can't tell whether it's layout, speed, forms or intent. Begin by isolating the mobile segment in analytics to size the gap and locate it, then watch mobile session recordings and heatmaps to see the cramped taps, mis-hit buttons and scrolling that numbers alone hide. Form analytics exposes where mobile input breaks down, and an on-site poll catches frustrations in the moment. Validate fixes in usability sessions run on real devices, not a shrunken desktop window.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Isolate the mobile segment to size the gap, then watch what the numbers hide.

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

- [Session Recordings](/research-methods/session-recordings)

- [Heatmaps](/research-methods/heatmaps)

### Focus
Expose where mobile input breaks down, and catch frustrations in the moment.

- [Form Analytics](/research-methods/form-analytics)

- [On-site Polls](/research-methods/on-site-polls)

### Validate
Test fixes in sessions run on real devices.

- [Remote Usability Studies](/research-methods/remote-usability-studies)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/mobile-experience
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Navigation & Information Architecture

**Visitors can't find the right product or page**

> I know what I want but the menus don't match how I think, so I keep hunting.

How might we structure navigation around how customers actually look for things?

## You'll recognise this when

- Heavy reliance on site search

- High pogo-sticking between category pages

- Low findability scores in past tests

## What this recipe does

Visitors know what they want but can't find it, so they bounce between pages or fall back on search and give up. Begin by reading the symptoms. Analytics surfaces the search terms and dead-end paths, and session recordings show the hunting behaviour in context. Then move to the structure itself, using card sorting to learn how customers expect content grouped and tree testing to check whether a proposed menu lets them find things. Validate the winning structure in usability sessions so you change the navigation on evidence rather than on internal logic.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Read the symptoms: search terms, dead-end paths, hunting behaviour.

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

- [Session Recordings](/research-methods/session-recordings)

### Focus
Learn how customers expect content grouped.

- [Card Sorting](/research-methods/card-sorting)

### Validate
Check the proposed structure lets people find things.

- [Tree Testing](/research-methods/tree-testing)

- [Remote Usability Studies](/research-methods/remote-usability-studies)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/navigation-information-architecture
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Onboarding & Activation Research

**New users don't reach first value**

> I signed up but couldn't quickly see the point, so I never really got started.

How might we get new users to their first win before they lose interest?

## You'll recognise this when

- High signup-to-activation drop-off

- Low day-7 return rate

- Early support tickets about getting started

## What this recipe does

New users sign up but never reach the first moment of real value, so they drift away before the product can prove itself. Analytics maps the activation funnel and the step where new users stall, and session recordings show what they try and abandon in those early minutes. Interviews and a survey explain what people expected and where reality fell short, while diary studies capture the experience across the first days rather than a single visit. Usability sessions on the onboarding flow then confirm whether a revised path gets people to value faster.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Map the activation funnel and watch the early minutes where users stall.

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

- [Session Recordings](/research-methods/session-recordings)

### Focus
Learn what people expected, and follow the experience across the first days.

- [Customer Interviews](/research-methods/customer-interviews)

- [Customer Survey](/research-methods/customer-survey)

- [Diary Studies](/research-methods/diary-studies)

### Validate
Confirm a revised onboarding path gets people to value faster.

- [Remote Usability Studies](/research-methods/remote-usability-studies)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/onboarding-activation
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Product Page Optimisation

**Product views don't turn into add-to-carts**

> I looked at the product but couldn't get the answers I needed to commit, so I left it.

How might we give product pages the information and reassurance that earns the add-to-cart?

## You'll recognise this when

- High product-page traffic with low add-to-cart rate

- Repeated pre-sales questions

- Attention stopping above key content

## What this recipe does

People reach the product page but don't add to basket, and it's unclear whether the blocker is information, doubt or price. Analytics shows how product pages perform relative to each other and where attention stops, while recordings and heatmaps reveal which content people seek out, skip or expand. On-site polls and a short survey draw out the unanswered questions and hesitations that hold a purchase back. Usability sessions then confirm whether a revised page actually resolves them, so the changes address real doubt rather than guesswork.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Compare product-page performance and see where attention stops.

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

- [Session Recordings](/research-methods/session-recordings)

- [Heatmaps](/research-methods/heatmaps)

### Focus
Draw out the unanswered questions and hesitations.

- [On-site Polls](/research-methods/on-site-polls)

- [Customer Survey](/research-methods/customer-survey)

### Validate
Confirm the revised page resolves real doubt.

- [Remote Usability Studies](/research-methods/remote-usability-studies)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/product-page
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Repeat Purchase & Post-Purchase Research

**First-time buyers never place a second order**

> The first order was fine. Nothing after it gave me a reason to order again.

How might we make the second order feel like the natural next step rather than a fresh decision?

## You'll recognise this when

- Revenue leans almost entirely on new-customer acquisition

- Repeat purchase rate stays flat while acquisition costs climb

- The post-purchase programme is an order confirmation and not much else

## What this recipe does

Most first-time buyers never come back, and the margin lives in the orders they never place. This recipe finds out why the second order isn't happening. Purchase cohort analysis shows the repeat rate, the typical gap to a second order, and which first products lead somewhere versus nowhere. The support team's structured input surfaces what buyers experience after checkout: delivery, returns, and the gap between the listing and the product in hand. One-time buyers explain why there was no second order, and repeat buyers explain what actually brought them back, which are rarely the same answer. Post-purchase and reorder concepts then get tested head to head with past buyers before the lifecycle programme is rebuilt around them.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Read the repeat rate, the gap to a second order, and what buyers experience after checkout.

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

- [Sales / Customer Service Survey](/research-methods/sales-customer-service-survey)

### Focus
Ask one-time buyers why there was no second order, and repeat buyers what brought them back.

- [Customer Survey](/research-methods/customer-survey)

- [Customer Interviews](/research-methods/customer-interviews)

### Validate
Test post-purchase and reorder concepts head to head with past buyers.

- [Preference Test](/research-methods/preference-test)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/repeat-purchase
Last updated: 2026-07-20


---

# Researching With Low Traffic

**We can't test because traffic is too low**

> We don't have the volume to be statistically significant, so every change is a leap of faith.

How might we build evidence for decisions when traffic can't support A/B tests?

## You'll recognise this when

- Sessions too low to reach significance in a realistic test window

- High-stakes pages with thin behavioural data

- Polls and analytics too sparse to read

- Decisions resting on opinion or the loudest voice

## What this recipe does

The site doesn't get enough traffic to run reliable A/B tests or gather meaningful poll and analytics data, so decisions default to opinion. This recipe builds evidence with methods that bring their own participants instead of borrowing yours.
A UX heuristic review and a competitor review set an expert baseline and show how others in the category solve the same problems, with no traffic required. Recruited-panel methods then carry the focus work: remote usability sessions show real people from your audience attempting the core journey, and copy testing checks the message lands with the people it is written for. Preference and prototype tests stand in for the A/B test at the validation step, weighing a proposed change against the current version with a recruited sample. The result is a decision backed by several independent signals, none of which needed the traffic you don't have.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

### Explore
Set an expert baseline and see how the category solves the same problems. No traffic required.

- [UX Heuristic Review](/research-methods/ux-heuristic-review)

- [Competitor Review](/research-methods/competitor-review)

### Focus
Let recruited panels carry the work: your audience, someone else's traffic.

- [Remote Usability Studies](/research-methods/remote-usability-studies)

- [Copy Testing](/research-methods/copy-testing)

### Validate
Stand in for the A/B test with recruited-sample comparisons.

- [Preference Test](/research-methods/preference-test)

- [Prototype Testing](/research-methods/prototype-testing)

Source: https://speero.com/research-recipes/researching-low-traffic
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# SaaS Pricing Page

**Buyers can't tell which plan fits them**

How might we help buyers self-select the right plan with confidence?

## You'll recognise this when

- High exit on the pricing page

- Low trial-to-paid

- Sales repeatedly answering the same plan-comparison questions

## What this recipe does

The pricing page is where SaaS buyers decide whether the product is worth it, and it is often where they stall. The goal is to understand why visitors hesitate, what they need in order to feel confident, and whether the plans, copy and layout match how they actually evaluate value.
Start broad with a competitor review and a UX heuristic review to see how rivals frame pricing and to surface obvious friction on your own page. Sales and customer service interviews bring in the real objections and questions buyers raise, which often explain hesitation the page never addresses. Copy testing checks whether plan names, feature descriptions and value framing are understood by the target audience. Remote usability studies then show how people move through the page and where they get stuck choosing a plan. The combination moves from market context, to internal knowledge, to message clarity, to observed behaviour, so no single lens carries the decision.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus. Validate.

See how rivals frame pricing and surface obvious friction on your own page.

Bring in the real objections buyers raise, and check the plan language is understood.

- [Sales / Customer Service Interviews](/research-methods/sales-customer-service-interviews)

- [Copy Testing](/research-methods/copy-testing)

### Validate
Watch how people move through the page and where they get stuck choosing.

- [Remote Usability Studies](/research-methods/remote-usability-studies)

How might we show up for the searches our best customers are already making, in their words rather than ours?

## You'll recognise this when

- Organic traffic is concentrated on branded terms

- Competitors hold the rankings for the problem-language queries

- Content ranks for informational terms that never convert

## What this recipe does

The customers who most need what the business does are searching for it in their own words and finding someone else. This recipe closes the language gap between how customers describe the problem and how the site describes the solution. Search data shows which intents the site is absent from and which rankings never earn the click, interviews surface the vocabulary customers actually use, and a review of the winning results pages shows what earning each intent takes. A glance test on the landing experience then confirms the click pays off before content investment scales. Search intent match is message match's organic twin.

# Traffic Quality & Channel Fit Research

**We're attracting the wrong visitors**

> The ad pulled me in but the offer wasn't what I actually wanted, so I left.

How might we attract visitors who match our best customers?

## You'll recognise this when

- High traffic with low qualified-lead rate

- Poor fit between ad audience and ICP

- Weak engagement from paid channels

## What this recipe does

Traffic is growing but the visitors arriving aren't the ones the business is built for, and everything downstream pays for it. This recipe works out where the misfit traffic enters and what it costs. Behavioural data shows which sources send visitors who bounce, stall or never return, CRM data shows which sources actually produce customers, the ads layer shows which campaigns and queries are buying the mismatch, and the sales floor tells you what a wrong-fit visitor sounds like. Panel message testing then checks that sharpened targeting and positioning reach the right people before more media spend follows the fix.

- [Sales / Customer Service Interviews](/research-methods/sales-customer-service-interviews)

### Validate
Test the sharpened who-this-is-for message before spend follows it.

- [Copy Testing](/research-methods/copy-testing)

# Free Trial to Paid Conversion

**Trial users don't convert to paid**

> I tried it during the trial but never hit the moment that made paying feel worth it.

How might we make the value obvious enough during the trial that paying feels like the natural next step?

## You'll recognise this when

- Low trial-to-paid rate

- Trial usage tailing off mid-trial

- Upgrade prompts ignored

- Discount requests clustering at trial end

## What this recipe does

People sign up for the trial but never convert to a paid plan, and the team can't tell whether the product failed to prove its value or the upgrade moment failed to land. Analytics maps what trial users actually do, separating those who convert from those who drift, and session recordings show the early sessions where the difference takes shape. Win-loss analysis of the CRM adds the pattern across accounts that upgraded and accounts that lapsed. An end-of-trial survey quantifies the leading reasons for not converting, and interviews with expired trials explain the gap between what people expected and what they experienced. Together these separate a value problem from a pricing or timing problem, which point to very different fixes.

## The method sequence

Explore. Focus.

### Explore
Map what trial users actually do, and watch the early sessions where converts and drifters diverge.

- [Analytics Data Analysis](/research-methods/analytics-data-analysis)

- [Session Recordings](/research-methods/session-recordings)

- [Win-loss Analysis (CRM Analysis)](/research-methods/win-loss-analysis)

### Focus
Quantify why trials lapse, and hear the expectation gap in users' own words.

- [Customer Survey](/research-methods/customer-survey)

- [Customer Interviews](/research-methods/customer-interviews)

Where's Validate? For this problem, validation lands in the experimentation programme itself: the hypotheses this research produces become A/B tests and product bets, measured against the outcome metric.

# Validating a Redesign Before Build

**A redesign is about to ship untested**

> As a visitor I'd be handed a new design the team hopes is better but hasn't checked with anyone like me.

How might we prove the new design beats the current one before we build it?

## You'll recognise this when

- Major redesign scoped

- Significant build cost

- No evidence the new direction outperforms the current page

## What this recipe does

A big redesign is about to be built and the risk is shipping months of work that performs worse than what it replaces. This recipe front-loads the validation. A five second test checks whether the new design communicates its point at a glance, a preference test weighs it against the current version, and copy testing pressure-tests the words carrying the message. Prototype and moderated usability sessions then confirm people can actually complete the core tasks, so the redesign earns its place before a developer touches it.

## The method sequence

Focus. Validate.

### Focus
Check the new design communicates its point, and pressure-test the words carrying it.

- [5 Second Test](/research-methods/five-second-test)

- [Copy Testing](/research-methods/copy-testing)

### Validate
Weigh it against the current version, confirm people can complete the core tasks, then prove it live.

- [Preference Test](/research-methods/preference-test)

- [Prototype Testing](/research-methods/prototype-testing)

- [Moderated Usability Studies](/research-methods/moderated-usability-studies)

- [A/B Testing](/research-methods/ab-testing)

# A/B Testing

Running a live, randomised experiment that splits traffic between a control and one or more variants to measure the causal effect of a change on a target metric.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Validate |
| Data type | Quantitative |
| Strength of signal | High |
| Effort | High |
| Surface area | Any surface |

## When to reach for it

Confirming that a change actually improves the outcome it targets before rolling it out fully. Settling disagreements about a design or flow with real customer behaviour rather than opinion.

## Strengths

Gives a direct, causal read on impact rather than a proxy signal. Removes bias from the decision since real customers self-select into each path.

## Limits

Needs enough traffic and time to reach a reliable result. Only tests the specific variants built, so it depends on earlier research to shape a strong hypothesis.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations
Best run once a hypothesis has already been shaped by exploratory and focus-stage research, since a test is only as good as the idea behind it.

## Common tools

Tools

- [AB Testing Tools (Speero Comparison)](https://speero.com/ab-testing-tools)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Checkout & Cart Optimisation](/research-recipes/checkout-cart-optimisation)

- [Landing Page Optimisation](/research-recipes/landing-page-optimisation)

- [Validating a Redesign Before Build](/research-recipes/validating-redesign)

## Go deeper

Go deeper

- [A/B testing tools comparison](https://speero.com/ab-testing-tools)

- [A/B test significance calculator](https://speero.com/ab-test-calculator)

- [How to prioritize your A/B test ideas](https://speero.com/post/how-to-prioritize-your-a-b-tests-ideas)

- [Can you run multiple A/B tests at the same time](https://speero.com/post/can-you-run-multiple-a-b-tests-at-the-same-time)

# Ads Analysis

Analysis of ads data within Google Ads, Facebook ads, Instagram ads, etc, focused on performance, CPC, Impressions, Clicks, Cost, with the aim of identifying which campaigns and ads are underperforming.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Focus |
| Data type | Quantitative |
| Strength of signal | High |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Acquisition & ads, Landing pages |

## When to reach for it

Increase your ROI from acquisition spendImprove the effectiveness of paid landing pagesStart optimising acquisition activitiesConnect your acquisition strategy to your on-site optimisation efforts

## Strengths

Analysing your ads data helps you to optimise spend by highlighting which campaigns are performing well, and which are not.

## Limits

Ads analysis on its own lacks qualitative insight needed to really determine why certain efforts are not performing.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Expertise
Ideally, you need someone with acquisition knowledge to conduct this activity, at the same time, you want someone who isn't directly involved in your acquisition strategy, to prevent bias.

# Analytics Data Analysis

Analysis of website analytics data to determine overall performance, performance by segment, e.g. device, channel, user type, analysis of on-site behaviour or digging into the impact a specific element or piece of functionality has on performance and user experience.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore, Focus, Validate |
| Data type | Quantitative |
| Strength of signal | High |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Any surface |

## When to reach for it

Understand overall on-site user behaviour with high levels of certainty (assuming no sampling) and the differences across key segments.
Dig deeper into the performance and / or impact of a specific page, element, or area of the website.

## Strengths

Analytics data is one of the most robust sources of data you can use to help you understand on-site engagement, interaction, and user behaviour. This is because this data is based on real user behaviour, without research bias, at a large scale.

## Limits

Sampling issues can reduce the accuracy of your data, which can result in drawing false assumptions, making decisions based on flawed data, etc.
Analytics data will tell you what is happening on your site, but not why. As with session recordings and heatmaps, the data is also open to interpretation.
Robust analytics data analysis is a skill. It can easily be misunderstood or misinterpreted.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Configuration
Effective analytics data analysis is reliant on a robust tool configuration, ensuring the data you're looking at is accurate. Effective set up can be complex and requires in-depth tool knowledge, ideally from a developer or from someone with experience in setting up analytics tools.

### Analysis
As analytics data is open to interpretation it is important to keep analysis actionable. At times it is relevant to simply point out facts, e.g. x% of data comes from mobile devices. But from an optimisation perspective, we should be considering the "so what?", e.g. what does this tell us, what opportunities does this present, etc?

### Tools
There are many digital analytics tools available. Chances are the business you work in or with will already use one. Google Analytics (now GA4) is one of the most popular and most well-known tools. The transition from Universal Analytics to GA4 happened in 2023 which significantly changed the way GA works.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Google Analytics](https://marketingplatform.google.com/about/analytics/)

- [Adobe Analytics](https://business.adobe.com/products/analytics/adobe-analytics.html)

- [Content Square](https://contentsquare.com)

- [Decibel Insight](https://www.medallia.com)

- [Heap](https://www.heap.io)

- [Full Story](https://www.fullstory.com)

- [Amplitude](/ab-testing-tools/amplitude)

# Brand Perception Survey

A structured survey run with a recruited panel that matches the target market, measuring unaided and aided brand awareness, brand preference, and the associations people hold against named competitors. Run before and after a brand change, the same instrument becomes a tracker. The baseline wave shows where perception stands, and later waves show whether it moved.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Focus, Validate |
| Data type | Quantitative / Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | Medium |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Messaging & copy, Acquisition & ads |

## When to reach for it

Establish a brand baseline before a rebrand, relaunch or repositioning, then re-measure after it ships.Find out whether the target market knows the brand exists, and what it is known for.See how perception and preference compare against named competitors in the consideration set.Track awareness and perception over time as a standing programme measure.

## Strengths

Recruited panels reach the people who don't know you, which the customer list never can, so awareness numbers stay honest.
Everything is measured against named competitors, so position is relative rather than absolute.
Repeatable. The same instrument re-run later gives a genuine before-and-after comparison.

## Limits

Panel quality decides everything. A panel that doesn't match the real buying audience measures the wrong people's opinions.
Perception moves slowly, so waves need spacing before the deltas mean anything.
It says what the market thinks, not what to change. It needs qualitative methods alongside it to explain the numbers.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Sampling
Survey the target market, not the customer base. Existing customers already know the brand, which inflates awareness and skews perception toward the product experience. Customers can be a separate, clearly labelled slice if their view is also wanted.

### Consistency
The value of tracking comes from asking the same questions of the same profile every wave. Resist rewording between waves, because every change breaks the comparison.

### Timing
Run the baseline before the brand change is announced, and leave enough time after launch for the market to notice before re-measuring.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Wynter](https://wynter.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Brand Perception Baseline & Tracking](/research-recipes/brand-perception-tracking)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/brand-perception-survey
Last updated: 2026-08-06


---

# Card Sorting

Card sorting involves participants sorting and labeling website content (which is represented on "cards") into groups that make sense to them. The data from all participants can then be combined to identify the core groupings, labels, and any anomalies. This data can be used to inform the structure of a website's navigation.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Focus, Validate |
| Data type | Quantitative |
| Strength of signal | Medium |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Navigation & IA |

## When to reach for it

Card sorting is a core part of designing and developing a website from scratch.
Card sorting can also be an effective research technique when other research has pointed to issues with how website content is grouped and labeled. This can help identify how users would expect content to be labeled and grouped, which can uncover optimization opportunities.

## Strengths

Card sorting is a relatively unique research method due to its focused nature (specifically focused on website content structure).
Card sorting provides insight into how users expect website content to be grouped and labeled.
You have the option of using open, closed, or hybrid card sorts, which can be beneficial in different ways at different points in a project.
Tools like OptimalWorkshop make remote card sorting relatively quick and easy to set up and run.

## Limits

Data analysis can be difficult/time intensive. The data provided by tools like OptimalWorkshop is extensive and although can be very insightful, it takes some understanding of the data to accurately interpret it.
Remote-moderated / Moderated card sorting is time-intensive and could be expensive.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Open vs. Closed
There are two different types of card sorting; open and closed. An open card sort. An open card sort allows participants to group and label all of the content as they wish, with no restrictions. A closed card sort involves participants grouping content under labels that you define. An open card sort therefore tends to be a more effective starting point. As you get closer to a defined set of labels, a closed card sort can be used to validate that users understand what content they would find under the labels you've defined. You can also use a hybrid approach where you define some category labels, but allow participants to also create their own. This can be beneficial when there are some categories that can't be changed for legal or technical reasons.

### Sample Size
Card sorting is primarily a quantitative method, and as such the sample size should be treated accordingly. NNGroup recommends 15 participants as a minimum, however, if you plan to run a quantitative style analysis then more is recommended.

### Remote, Remote-moderated, Moderated
Card sorting can be conducted in various ways, similar to usability studies (Remote, Remote-moderated, Moderated). The benefit to Remote-Moderated or Moderated is that you are able to gather some qualitative insights as well as the data on the final groups and labels. For example, you'll be able to see when a participant is unsure where to group or how to label, you can find out what is making them unsure. This insight can highlight the content that could be most difficult to find an intuitive home for within the website structure.

### Tools
For remote or remote-moderated, there are a wide range of online tools available. OptimalWorkshop specializes in card sorting and tree testing, but you can also use tools such as Userlytics and Usabilityhub. The benefit of a tool like OptimalWorkshop is the extensive data available for analysis. For moderated card sorting you can either set up a computer and have participants conduct the card sort on a screen using one of these tools, or, you can use physical tools, e.g. post-it notes and pens. Using physical tools has the benefit of the participant feeling more free to move cards around, try different labels, etc. however, the data analysis is more challenging as you'd need to manually add the results from each participant into a tool in order to access the data. Moderated card sorting is also much more time intensive.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Optimal Workshop](https://www.optimalworkshop.com)

- [Userlytics](https://www.userlytics.com)

- [Usability Hub](https://www.lyssna.com)

- [UserZoom](https://www.usertesting.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Navigation & Information Architecture](/research-recipes/navigation-information-architecture)

## Go deeper

Go deeper

- [Card sorting, uncover users' mental models (NN/g)](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-definition/)

- [Card sorting vs tree testing (NN/g)](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-tree-testing-differences/)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/card-sorting
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Competitor Review

A competitor review involves reviewing the website UX of your competitors, using the UX heuristic principles,  to help gather an understanding of the market/industry, identify trends, gather inspiration and compare the user experience to the client’s website.
A competitor review could also include review of the competitor's offering, pricing and overall proposition, to gather an understanding of the industry and identify opportunities.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore, Focus |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | Low |
| Effort | Low |
| Surface area | Any surface |

## When to reach for it

A competitor analysis can be beneficial to understand the different user experiences your potential customers may be exposed to in their comparison process.
If you're struggling to solve a specific problem that is very specific to your industry, it can be beneficial to understand how others in your industry solve these problems.
If you're new to a role / industry then a competitor review can be beneficial to give you an overview of the industry and the competition. It's good practice to keep up to speed with what competitors are doing, but it should not side track you from focusing on solving your own business challenges.

## Strengths

Understand the wider industry, who is doing what and where you sit within this (from a UX, price, offering and proposition perspective).
Gather ideas and inspiration about how to tackle key customer problems.

## Limits

Just because a competitor is doing something, does not mean it is working for them. It is important not to blindly copy competitors, but to use the insights as inspiration.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Which competitors?
You can include as many competitors as you have time for in your competitor review. Typically, we would review between 3-5. You may also want to consider including companies outside your "typical" competitor set, but who offer a solution to a shared customer problem, or have similar challenges (even if they are actually in a different industry/sector).

## Common tools

Tools

- [Miro](https://miro.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Researching With Low Traffic](/research-recipes/researching-low-traffic)

- [SEO & Search Intent Research](/research-recipes/seo-search-intent)

- [Trust & Credibility Audit](/research-recipes/trust-credibility)

# Copy Testing

A form of user research focused on website copy and written content. A sample pool of users are recruited and asked to review excerpts of copy. They are then asked to answer a series of questions to assess their level of understanding, outstanding questions and next steps. Our recommended copy testing tool is Wynter.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore, Focus, Validate |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | Medium |
| Effort | Low |
| Surface area | Messaging & copy, Landing pages, Pricing page |

## When to reach for it

Understand how your audience perceives your messaging- Is anything confusing or unclear?- Is there something that doesn’t make sense or misses the mark?
Validate your audience’s pain points.- Do they feel your company understands their needs and solves their problems?
Define the benefits that resonate the most with your audience.- What benefits are they most interested in?- What benefits are they least interested in?
Stand out from the competition- You can identify if the headline resonates with the target audience, if they find it unique or bland.

## Strengths

You can outsource the participants, meaning that you don’t need:- to implement any new tools on your actual website.- a lot of visitors on your site, or existing customers to get started.
Gather qualitative feedback on the website copy and content.
Recruit people who match your ICP.

## Limits

Copy testing is focused only on copy, you can't / shouldn't use this method to gather insights about design or functionality.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Recruitment
You need to consider who is your target audience and ensure that the participants match your ICP. You should evaluate if the tool you are going to use will help you find relevant participants in the right audience, or if you can find those participants elsewhere.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Wynter](https://wynter.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [B2B ICP Research](/research-recipes/b2b-icp-research)

- [Brand Perception Baseline & Tracking](/research-recipes/brand-perception-tracking)

- [Content-to-Lead Conversion Research](/research-recipes/content-to-lead)

- [Involuntary Churn & Payment Recovery Research](/research-recipes/involuntary-churn)

- [Landing Page Optimisation](/research-recipes/landing-page-optimisation)

- [Lead Quality Research](/research-recipes/lead-quality)

- [Trust & Credibility Audit](/research-recipes/trust-credibility)

- [Validating a Redesign Before Build](/research-recipes/validating-redesign)

- [Value Proposition & Messaging](/research-recipes/value-prop-messaging)

## Go deeper

# Customer Interviews

Usually 30 minute - 1 hour sessions run on a one-to-one basis either in person or remotely on Zoom, Teams, etc. Customers are recruited via email database and should ideally be incentivized for their time, e.g. a discount code or gift card.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore, Focus |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | Medium |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Any surface, Messaging & copy |

## When to reach for it

To understand customers motivations, FUDs (fears, uncertainties, and doubts) perception of your product/service, to understand what problem/s your product/service solves for them and any improvement areas based on their experiences.
Customer interviews can also be used to investigate specific topics or areas of opportunity.

## Strengths

Customer interviews allow you to dig deeper than customer surveys by asking follow up questions based on customers answers. This makes them more appropriate for more complex use cases or when you have a more specific area of focus.

## Limits

Customer interviews can be time-consuming, which means they are not effective for gathering large samples of data (unless you have a large budget / a lot of time resources). To help mitigate this, customer interviews can be used alongside a customer survey to gather both in-depth, high quality insights at a large scale.
An insightful customer interview is determined by the questions you ask. Much like running moderated usability studies, there is skill involved inrunning an effective customer interview. You need to avoid leading questions, and also ensure questions are not multifaceted as this can cause difficulty in analysis.
Customer interviews should not be used to gather feedback into website user experiences. Asking users to recall their experiences of your website is likely to gather invalid data. If you're looking for UX insights, a moderated usability study would be more appropriate (note: these methods can also be combined into a hybrid interview with some usability study tasks).
Gathering data from existing (or lapsed) customers will always have an element of bias, since these people have pre-conceptions of your brand / product / service based on their experiences. This is okay as long as you are aware of this and mitigate it accordingly, e.g. by also running research with people who have never heard of or used your brand / product / service before. For more focused research, in some cases using existing customers will be more relevant, whereas in others, using new users will be more appropriate.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Recruitment
The most effective recruitment method for existing customers is to reach out to your existing email database of customers. You should consider the types of customers you want to speak to when deciding who to email, e.g. recent convertors, loyal customers, lapsed customers, etc. Who you speak to will influence the output, so this should be based around your research goal. If you're running top-level exploratory research, then start with recent convertors, however if you are running interviews with a more focused objective, use this to determine who you reach out to.

### Incentive
An incentive can be used to help boost the response rate. This could be in the form of a discount code or gift card. The amount and type of incentive should be determined by the type of people you are trying to reach, e.g. B2B vs. B2C, age, household income, job title / position, etc. Also consider what you are asking of them, e.g. 30 minutes or 1 hour, the incentive should be reflective of the time they are giving you.

### Logistics
If you're recruiting customers for interviews and planning the sessions yourself, there are a few logistics to keep in mind;

- Booking a timeslot; before you send the initial email asking for people to take part, consider how you'll organise the sessions. You could share a Calendly link or something similar to allow customers to book directly with you. Whatever you use, you want to avoid having to manually agree on a date / time by going back and forth via email.

- Tool; if you're not including any usability study tasks in your interview then you can effectively use any video conferencing tool (Zoom, Teams, Hangouts, etc). Don't forget to record the sessions (but ask permission first) to ensure you don't have to write everything down when you're running the interview.

- No shows; especially when recruiting yourself, there's a relatively high chance of no-shows. Consider how to mitigate this, for example, sending out a series of reminders in the days / hours running up to the session, as well as over recruiting (e.g. running 1-2 more sessions than you need). Mention in your comms that you will wait for 10 minutes before assuming a no-show, so you don't have to sit and wait for the full amount of time until they turn up.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Zoom](https://zoom.us)

- [Lookback](https://www.lookback.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [B2B ICP Research](/research-recipes/b2b-icp-research)

- [Churn & Retention Research](/research-recipes/churn-retention)

- [Engagement Decay & Habit Research](/research-recipes/engagement-decay)

- [Free Trial to Paid Conversion](/research-recipes/trial-to-paid)

- [Lead Quality Research](/research-recipes/lead-quality)

- [Onboarding & Activation Research](/research-recipes/onboarding-activation)

- [Repeat Purchase & Post-Purchase Research](/research-recipes/repeat-purchase)

- [SEO & Search Intent Research](/research-recipes/seo-search-intent)

- [Trust & Credibility Audit](/research-recipes/trust-credibility)

- [Value Proposition & Messaging](/research-recipes/value-prop-messaging)

## Go deeper

Go deeper

- [Deep ICP research](https://speero.com/post/deep-icp-research)

- [4 mental models for voice of customer research](https://speero.com/post/4-mental-models-to-help-you-conduct-voice-of-customer-research)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/customer-interviews

# Customer Survey

A customer survey sent out via email to your customers (ideally segmented by customer type, e.g. new customers, recently lapsed customers, VIPs, etc). Typically the goal of a customer survey is to understand customers perception of your product/service, to understand what problem/s your product/service solves for them and any improvement areas based on their experiences.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore, Focus |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | Medium |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Any surface, Messaging & copy |

## When to reach for it

To understand customers motivations, FUDs (fears, uncertainties, and doubts) perception of your product/service, to understand what problem/s your product/service solves for them and any improvement areas based on their experiences.
Customer surveys can also be used to investigate specific topics or areas of opportunity.

## Strengths

A customer survey allows you to gather large samples of data, which isn't possible when running customer interviews. Customer surveys can also be used alongside customer interviews to increase the depth of insight.
Customer surveys can be used to gather valuable insight into wider business strategy, as well as what is important to users in general when considering products/services like yours.
Customer surveys allow you to gather both qualitative and quantitative data, depending on the types of questions you ask.

## Limits

An insightful customer survey is determined by the questions you ask. you need to avoid leading questions, and also ensure questions are not multifaceted as this can cause difficulty in analysis.
Customer surveys should not be used to gather feedback into website user experiences. Asking users to recall their experiences of your website is likely to gather invalid data.
It can be a challenge to code and analyse large sets of qualitative data.
Gathering data from existing (or lapsed) customers will always have an element of bias, since these people have pre-conceptions of your brand / product / service based on their experiences. This is okay as long as you are aware of this and mitigate it accordingly, e.g. by also running research with people who have never heard of or used your brand / product / service before. For more focused research, in some cases using existing customers will be more relevant, whereas in others, using new users will be more appropriate.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Tool
The survey could be built in a range of tools, including Google Forms, TypeForm, Survey Monkey, etc. There are plenty of free tools available for this activity, so there's not really any need to pay for a tool, unless you have more bespoke needs, e.g. large data sets, custom question logic, etc.

### Incentive
An incentive can be used to help boost the response rate. This could be in the form of a discount code or gift card. The amount and type of incentive should be determined by the type of people you are trying to reach, e.g. B2B vs. B2C, age, household income, job title / position, etc.

### Sample Size
You need approximately 200 open-ended responses to be confident in the strength of signal within the analysis (have a 95% confidence that the answer strength of the signal is valid within ~5-10% of what is reported).

## Common tools

Tools

- [TypeForm](https://www.typeform.com)

- [Google Forms](https://www.google.com/forms/about/)

- [Survey Monkey](https://www.surveymonkey.com)

- [Userback.io](https://userback.io)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Conversion Research](/research-recipes/conversion-research)

- [Free Trial to Paid Conversion](/research-recipes/trial-to-paid)

- [Involuntary Churn & Payment Recovery Research](/research-recipes/involuntary-churn)

- [Onboarding & Activation Research](/research-recipes/onboarding-activation)

- [Repeat Purchase & Post-Purchase Research](/research-recipes/repeat-purchase)

- [Trust & Credibility Audit](/research-recipes/trust-credibility)

- [Value Proposition & Messaging](/research-recipes/value-prop-messaging)

## Go deeper

Go deeper

- [4 mental models for voice of customer research](https://speero.com/post/4-mental-models-to-help-you-conduct-voice-of-customer-research)

# Diary Studies

Diary studies involve recruiting participants to take part in research over the period of a few weeks to a few months. Participants are asked to submit "diary" entries every time they naturally do a certain behaviour, e.g. browse for a specific product or service. Diary studies can be conducted via email, text, whatsapp or bespoke platforms.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore, Focus |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | High |
| Effort | High |
| Surface area | Any surface |

## When to reach for it

Used to collect qualitative data about user behaviors, activities, and experiences over time. This is appropriate only in cases where the decision making process is particularly long, and there is a need to understand the wider user journey / key touchpoints.
Relevant sectors could be the automotive or property industries. Diary studies could also be effective when looking to gather insight into offline parts of the journey, e.g. the returns process.

## Strengths

Diary studies are a in-depth longitudinal research study, as such you can gather robust data about the wider user journey and decision-making process. These insights are difficult to gather using any other method.

## Limits

Diary studies can be long and complex to conduct. The exact length will depend on the typical decision-making process, e.g. buying a car or a house.
Diary studies can be expensive since you need to recruit carefully (people who are genuinely in the market for these products or services) and incentivize generously (since these participants could be part of the research study for weeks or months).

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Incentives
It is advisable to think about offering a staged incentive. E.g. 50% upfront, 50% on completion. This ensures participants continue engaging with the research project all the way through.

### Tools
There are many tools you could use to gather "diary entries" on an ongoing basis. You could use text, Whatsapp, or email. Alternatively use a specific diary study tool. The key consideration here is to use a method that is as easy as possible for the participant to input an entry, if they have to log into a specific tool everytime, they may be less inclined to submit an entry vs. using Whatsapp.

## Common tools

Tools
Runs on your existing systems; no dedicated tool required.

## Recipes that use this method

- [Engagement Decay & Habit Research](/research-recipes/engagement-decay)

- [Onboarding & Activation Research](/research-recipes/onboarding-activation)

## Go deeper

Go deeper

- [Diary studies, understanding long-term user behaviour (NN/g)](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/)

- [When to use context methods, field and diary studies (NN/g)](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/context-methods-field-diary-studies/)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/diary-studies
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# 5 Second Test

We use a sample pool of target participants and analyse their responses to a series of questions after they look at a page for a limited time (typically 5 seconds). This helps us gather feedback on the copy, UI, clarity/motivation on next action etc. Five second tests allow us to gauge what information and impression users derive from a design within the initial five seconds of viewing the page. This helps us understand the effectiveness of the design and the messaging.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Validate, Focus |
| Data type | Quantitative |
| Strength of signal | Low |
| Effort | Low |
| Surface area | Landing pages, Messaging & copy |

## When to reach for it

The primary use case for a 5 second test is to gather insight into users very first impression of a page. This could be as part of research on landing page optimisation and / or acquisition research.
5 second testing could also be used as part of validation research. If you want to establish how a change to a page, such as a headline copy change, will change users first impressions.
5 second tests are best for gathering insights about copy and overall page design / messaging.

## Strengths

5 second testing is a quick and inexpensive way to gather insight into users first impressions of a page.

## Limits

The nature of a 5 second test means there's only so much value you can gain. 5 seconds is not a long time, and it's likely the participant will only be able to answer 1 or 2 core questions.
5 second tests are conducted on screenshots / designs, meaning participants can't interact with functionality.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Tools
There are many tools that provide 5 second tests as a service, including Usabilityhub and Maze.

### Sample Size
Ideally, each test would have about 50 -100 participants to maintain the quality of insights. The number of participants can increase or decrease depending on the number of segments of users you are targeting (ex: mobile and desktop tests require at least 50 participants each).

### Length
It is possible to increase the length of a 5 second test, e.g. to 10 or 15 seconds. In some cases it could be beneficial to slightly increase the length of time the participant sees the page for, to ensure they have adequate time to answer the follow up questions effectively.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Usability Hub](https://www.lyssna.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Acquisition Research](/research-recipes/acquisition-research)

- [Content-to-Lead Conversion Research](/research-recipes/content-to-lead)

- [Landing Page Optimisation](/research-recipes/landing-page-optimisation)

- [SEO & Search Intent Research](/research-recipes/seo-search-intent)

- [Validating a Redesign Before Build](/research-recipes/validating-redesign)

- [Value Proposition & Messaging](/research-recipes/value-prop-messaging)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/five-second-test
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Form Analytics

Form analytics is similar to regular analytics analysis, but focused on your website forms.  You can analyse metrics such as form field interaction, drop out rates, error rates, etc to understand which fields are causing friction.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Focus, Explore |
| Data type | Quantitative |
| Strength of signal | High |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Forms, Checkout & cart |

## When to reach for it

Exploratory research has identified a specific barrier in your checkout or on other onsite forms.

## Strengths

Provides in-depth data to inform form optimisation; e.g. removing fields, changing layouts etc.

## Limits

Can be subject to technical issues, much like standard analytics tools, the accuracy of the configuration is integral.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Tools
You can either set this up manually using custom analytics tracking or using a bespoke Form analytics tool, like Zuko.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Zuko](https://www.zuko.io)
