# Heatmaps

Heat maps visualise on-site behaviour by representing clicks, hover and mouse movement with colours overlaid on a screenshot of the pages of a website. In general red indicates an area of high engagement (either clicks, hovers, or mouse movement) and blue indicates "cold" areas of low engagement. Heat maps are generated by a tool added into your website code. Heat map tools include Hotjar, Content Square and Full Story.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore, Focus, Validate |
| Data type | Quantitative |
| Strength of signal | Medium |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Any surface |

## When to reach for it

Visualise how users behave on specific pages on the website. Understand which elements on the page are drawing users attention and which are being missed. Dig deeper into friction points / engagement with specific pages/elements.
Heatmap analysis can be beneficial for gathering an overall understanding of how users are interacting with your website, as well as digging into interactions with specific pages or elements.
Heatmaps can also be used to compare on-page behaviour between different variations of an experiment, which can be beneficial from an analysis perspective.

## Strengths

Visualise real on-page behaviour with no research bias; users don't specifically know they are being recorded.
Helps bring other data such as digital analytics numbers "to life", by providing a more visual representation of the data. For example, Analytics might show a high exit rate from the basket page, session recordings can help explain why this is happening by showing users interacting with the basket (and potentially experiencing issues).
Heatmaps are an amalgamation of group behaviour, e.g. they represent trends from a large sample of users. As such, you can analyse large scale user behaviour relatively easily.

## Limits

Heat maps are open to interpretation, since there's a lack of explanation of the behaviour. You may see high or low engagement with a specific element, but you won't necessarily know why there is high or low engagement.
Heat maps can be prone to technical issues. It's important to be aware of the types of issues that can occur, for example, usually the tool will take a screenshot of the page from the sample user and then overlay the data which represents 100s or 1000s of users on that screenshot. That screenshot may not be representative of exactly what every user sees. Dynamic elements can also cause technical issues with heat maps; e.g. you may see high engagement on the main homepage banner, but this could actually represent engagement with the main navigation drop-downs. It's important not to take everything you see as 100% truth, if you see something unusual or that you can't explain, it may be indicative of a technical issue that should be investigated.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Analysis & Interpretation
As with session recordings, it can be beneficial to gather multiple people together for analysis and interpretation of heatmaps to hypothesise about why this behaviour might be happening. Since there is no way of knowing the truth at this stage, it can help to have multiple points of view.

### Tools
Tools include Hotjar, Content Square, Full Story and Microsoft Clarity. These tools have a very wide range of price points, typically Hotjar was the tool of choice due to it's reasonable price point, but this has increased in price more recently. Microsoft Clarity offers a free solution.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Hotjar](https://www.hotjar.com)

- [Content Square](https://contentsquare.com)

- [Decibel Insight](https://www.medallia.com)

- [Microsoft Clarity](https://clarity.microsoft.com)

- [VWO](/ab-testing-tools/vwo)

- [Full Story](https://www.fullstory.com)

- [Mouseflow](https://mouseflow.com)

- [Crazyegg](https://www.crazyegg.com)

- [Lucky Orange](https://www.luckyorange.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Category & Listing Page Optimisation](/research-recipes/category-listing-page)

- [Checkout & Cart Optimisation](/research-recipes/checkout-cart-optimisation)

- [Content-to-Lead Conversion Research](/research-recipes/content-to-lead)

- [Conversion Research](/research-recipes/conversion-research)

# Live Chat Analysis

Analysis of on-site live chat transcripts to uncover fears, uncertainties and doubts that users are facing on-site, including identifying any unanswered questions (which could point towards missing or sub-optimal website content).

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | Medium |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Any surface |

## When to reach for it

If you have live chat on-site and get high volumes of engagement, then analysing the questions users are asking can be a goldmine of insights.
If you have limited time and budget to conduct new research then analysing live chat data is a really effective way to tap into users main queries and struggles.

## Strengths

No need to conduct new research / collect data & insights.
Gather insights from real users who have a genuine need for your product or service.
Understand the key questions and barriers holding users back from converting.

## Limits

Can be time-consuming if you have a lot of data to analyse; equally, the value can decrease if you have limited data.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Sample Size
As with surveys and polls, the sweet spot for analysis of live chat data is between 200-300 responses.

### Live Chat type
The value of this data will depend on the type of live chat you have. E.g. a chatbot vs. a manned live chat. How you approach analysis will depend on what data you collect and in what format, for example, if the customer service team categorise the query or not.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Lucky Orange](https://www.luckyorange.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Churn & Retention Research](/research-recipes/churn-retention)

- [Involuntary Churn & Payment Recovery Research](/research-recipes/involuntary-churn)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/live-chat-analysis
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Moderated Usability Studies

Use a sample pool of participants who match your target audience. Watch and listen as they walk through your site and perform queued tasks. Moderated usability studies involve one-to-one sessions conducted by a skilled moderator who will set the tasks and questions, allowing for a deeper level of insight. Moderated usability studies can be conducted in person or via Zoom, Teams, etc.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore, Focus |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | High |
| Effort | High |
| Surface area | Any surface |

## When to reach for it

A requirement to understand the wider user journey, e.g. how users shop / browse more generally. A need for more in-depth, qualitative insights, a longer / more detailed user journey / set of tasks (that would be difficult to explain in a remote setting).

## Strengths

Moderated usability studies give more control to the moderator, since they are running the session live. This means they can answer questions from the participant and / or bring the participant back on track if they get stuck or misunderstand the task.
The insights from moderated usability studies tend to be more in-depth than those from remote. Again, this is because the moderator is able to ask follow-up questions, ask for clarification, etc.

## Limits

The success of moderated usability studies is dependent on the skills of the moderator. Sessions can be subject to bias if moderators ask leading questions or tasks.
Sessions can also be subject to bias such as the Hawthorne effect, since the participants are being observed live.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Tool
There are many remote usability study tools, with slightly different capabilities and pricing models. Much like with AB testing tools, the success of your research is not necessarily determined by the tool you use, but by what you do with it (e.g. accurate recruitment, well-crafted tasks, and questions, etc). Key considerations when picking a tool include; the size and quality of their participant panel, the ability to add a recruitment screener, the analysis capabilities, what's included (e.g. participant incentives). Also double check how their pricing works, e.g. does it scale up based on the recruitment criteria and estimated length of session. Most tools now offer the option to set up and recruit for moderated usability studies in a similar way to remote; you will specify the moderator's availability and suitable participants will book in to the available slots.

### Recruitment
For moderated usability studies, a tool like Userlytics or Usertesting.com is not always necessary. You can use another recruitment method and use  any video call tool to run the sessions. Alternative recruitment methods include recruiting from existing customer database, or recruiting via an on-site poll. But be careful, as doing it this way increases the chance of no-shows, it also requires some admin from your side in terms of booking in sessions and paying incentives.

### Sample Size
Nielsen Norman says "The answer is 5, except when it's not" regarding usability study sample size. We use this as a guide; but one that should be considered rather than followed blindly. For example, if you're testing on multiple devices or with different user types, then you need to apply this rule to all of those segments. You may also want to add 1-2 additional "buffer" sessions to account for poorer quality participants, tech issues, no shows, etc.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Zoom](https://zoom.us)

- [Askable](https://askable.com)

- [UserZoom](https://www.usertesting.com)

- [Lookback](https://www.lookback.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Validating a Redesign Before Build](/research-recipes/validating-redesign)

## Go deeper

Go deeper

- [How to get the most out of your user testing efforts](https://speero.com/post/how-to-get-the-most-out-of-your-user-testing-efforts)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/moderated-usability-studies

# On-site Polls

On-site polls are very short surveys that appear on your website for website users to answer. They are typically made up of 1-2 questions (since it is important not to disrupt the user journey). These can be open or closed questions, depending on the research objective. On-site polls can be run site wide or on specific pages, and can be triggered on a range of behaviours such as time on site / page, scroll depth and exit intent (on desktop).

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore, Focus |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | Medium |
| Effort | Low |
| Surface area | Any surface |

## When to reach for it

Gather feedback as users are experiencing a website to help understand key barriers from users who haven’t converted yet. This makes them an effective method for gathering insight into UX friction and barriers to conversion. On-site polls can also be used to understand more about external factors, such as intent or motivation for visiting the website, or to understand more about the types of people visiting the website.
You can also be creative with the way you use on-site polls; for example you could use an on-site poll to recruit users for other research methods such as interviews or usability studies. This can be particularly useful when looking to target users who have a genuine need for your product or service, but who have not yet converted.

## Strengths

On-site polls provide insight from users who have naturally found their way to your website, meaning they have a genuine need for your product or service.
By their nature, on-site polls allow you to gather insight there and then while the user is interacting with your website. This means feedback is almost immediate and prevents the user having to recall their previous experiences (which can introduce a lot of bias).

## Limits

The main downfall of on-site polls is the disruption they can cause to the user experience. By appearing potentially mid-way through their journey, a poll could frustrate or disrupt, which could negatively impact brand perception and likelihood to convert. This can be somewhat mitigated by using logical poll design, e.g. making the pop up relatively subtle, using colours that match the website look and feel, etc. You should also consider what other pop ups you may have on your website. If you already have other pop ups such as offers, live chat, etc. then adding another pop up could exacerbate users frustration.
The response rate is often relatively low. When planning your poll you should expect less than 10% response rate. You need to look at your current traffic levels and poll triggers to determine how long your poll will need to run. If you're going to have to run a poll any longer than 4 weeks to reach a minimum of 200 responses, then a poll may not be the most suitable research method for you.
The nature of on-site pop ups (and their propensity to cause frustration) can sometimes mean a high amount of "spam" responses. This means users who simply answer to get rid of the pop up, or answer saying "this pop up" is their main frustration (don't be surprised to see some swear words within the responses!) Review your responses and filter out any spam before ending a poll, ensuring you have reached your sample size with quality responses.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Questions / Logic
There are different ways to approach on-site poll question design. Some schools of thought suggest that asking an "easy" question first, such as a closed Y/N question, can help "hook" users into answering more open questions. For example, "Can you find all the information you're looking for on this page?". However, in reality, there is often a large drop-off in response rate between the first and any subsequent questions. You need to consider the impact of this, e.g. you may come away with only insight on the % of users who answered Yes and No, which is not necessarily actionable.
As such, you may wish to start with a more open question. This may reduce overall response rate but increase the quality of the insight, e.g. "What information, if any, is missing from this page?". But again, by asking this, you won't gather the top-level data on no. of Yes or No responses.
An effective method is to run a series of polls. E.g. start with "Can you find all the information you're looking for on this page?". Then, once you have gathered sufficient data, run a second poll "What information, if any, is missing from this page?" It may be that a high percentage of respondents answered the first poll with "Yes", which could suggest that the information on the page is sufficient and efforts may be best used elsewhere.

### Tools
Hotjar is one of the most popular tools for running on-site polls, due to its relatively cost-effective pricing model (although this has changed somewhat over recent months). There are many tools available with differing capabilities. When considering a tool the main factor to think about is the triggering capabilities; you want flexibility in who and how you target the poll to ensure you gather the most relevant insights.

### Sample Size
We need approximately 200 open-ended responses to be confident in our strength of signal within the analysis (have a 95% confidence that the answer strength of the signal is valid within ~5-10% of what is reported).

## Common tools

Tools

- [Hotjar](https://www.hotjar.com)

- [VWO](/ab-testing-tools/vwo)

- [Medallia](https://www.medallia.com)

- [Userback.io](https://userback.io)

- [Lucky Orange](https://www.luckyorange.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [B2B ICP Research](/research-recipes/b2b-icp-research)

- [Category & Listing Page Optimisation](/research-recipes/category-listing-page)

- [Checkout & Cart Optimisation](/research-recipes/checkout-cart-optimisation)

- [Content-to-Lead Conversion Research](/research-recipes/content-to-lead)

- [Conversion Research](/research-recipes/conversion-research)

- [Landing Page Optimisation](/research-recipes/landing-page-optimisation)

- [Lead-Gen Form Optimisation](/research-recipes/lead-gen-form)

# Online Review Analysis

Structured analysis of the reviews the market has already written on review platforms, app stores and marketplaces, for the brand and for its competitors. Mining the text surfaces recurring praise, complaints, feature language and switching triggers, in the reviewers' own words.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | Low |
| Effort | Low |
| Surface area | Any surface, Messaging & copy |

## When to reach for it

Learn the strengths and weaknesses the market volunteers about the brand and its competitors.Harvest the vocabulary reviewers use, for messaging, copy testing and search work.Spot the recurring reasons people switch toward or away from a product.Build competitor understanding without recruiting a single participant.

## Strengths

The data already exists, so it is fast to start and there is no recruitment.
Competitor reviews are as accessible as your own, which is rare in research.
Reviewers explain their reasoning in their own words, giving quotable, specific language.

## Limits

Reviews cluster at the extremes, because the satisfied middle rarely writes.
Platform incentives and vendor review programmes shape what gets posted.
Reviews describe the product experience more than the brand, so they inform perception work without measuring awareness.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Source selection
Match platforms to the category. Software lives on software review sites, consumer products on marketplaces and app stores. Note each platform's review-collection incentives when weighing what you read.

### Recency
Weight recent reviews more heavily. Old reviews describe a product and a market that may no longer exist.

## Common tools

Tools

- [G2](https://www.g2.com)

- [Trustpilot](https://www.trustpilot.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Brand Perception Baseline & Tracking](/research-recipes/brand-perception-tracking)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/online-review-analysis
Last updated: 2026-08-06

# Preference Test

Preference testing involves showing participants two (or more) versions of a page, an element, or a piece of copy, and asking them to select their preference and provide rationale for their preference. Data from the full sample of participants can then be used to draw conclusions about the best-performing version.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Validate |
| Data type | Quantitative |
| Strength of signal | Low |
| Effort | Low |
| Surface area | Any surface |

## When to reach for it

Preference tests are a validation technique designed to gather data on a concept or solution. As such, preference tests can be beneficial in the planning stages of an AB test to either pre-validate or refine test concepts. Preference tests can also be used as an alternative to an AB test where true AB testing isn't possible for technical reasons or where there's not enough traffic.

## Strengths

Preference testing is generally quick and inexpensive, providing a quick and easy way to gather data to help inform concept design.

## Limits

Participants can't interact with functionality in a preference test. This means feedback is focused on the design, look and feel of the page, rather than being a true assessment of ease of use. This makes the method more suitable when the required feedback is based on the design or page copy, rather than the functionality or ease of use.
Despite similarities with a true AB test, preference testing is subject to some research bias, since participants are not truly visiting your website or parting with their data/money.
The low time investment from participants and thus the low level of incentive can impact the quality of the responses. It's important to review any qualitative feedback to help identify void responses.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Sample Size
Preference tests gather quantitative data, as such the sample size should be large enough to draw robust conclusions. We would recommend including at least 30 participants (ideally more).

### Tools
There are many preference testing tools. Typically this is an option built into tools like Maze, Usabilityhub and Wynter, rather than there being stand-alone tools. Maze and Usabilityhub are focused on design preference tests, whereas Wynter is focused on copy preference tests.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Usability Hub](https://www.lyssna.com)

- [Wynter](https://wynter.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Repeat Purchase & Post-Purchase Research](/research-recipes/repeat-purchase)

- [Researching With Low Traffic](/research-recipes/researching-low-traffic)

- [Validating a Redesign Before Build](/research-recipes/validating-redesign)

## Go deeper

Go deeper

- [https://maze.co/blog/preference-testing/](https://maze.co/blog/preference-testing/)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/preference-test
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Prototype Testing

Use usability study tools or specific prototype testing tools such as Maze to set recruited participants specific tasks to complete on a prototype version of a page, functionality or website. This is usually conducted remotely (see remote usability studies) but can also be in a moderated setting.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Validate |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | Medium |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Any surface |

## When to reach for it

To validate that a proposed solution has the intended impact in improving the user experience. Identify any issues pre-development.

## Strengths

Gather qualitative data to support a design or functionality change before (or instead of) AB testing.
Prototype testing is beneficial when you can't AB test due to technical restrictions or traffic limitations.
Prototype testing tools tend to be relatively inexpensive.

## Limits

Creating a prototype for testing can be time-intensive, depending on the functionality you're testing.
If you're going on to AB test as well running prototype testing will slow down the process of getting test results.
Technical issues with the prototype during the sessions can negatively impact the validity of the insights.
As with usability studies, you need to consider the wording used in your questions and tasks, to prevent leading participants and invalidating your insights.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Tools
You can use any usability study method or tool to run prototype testing, such as remote, remote moderated, moderated, Userlytics, Usertesting.com, etc. You can also use a specific prototype testing tool, such as Maze.

### Sample size
The same logic as usability studies applies here. Nielsen Norman says "The answer is 5, except when it's not" regarding usability study sample size. We use this as a guide; but one that should be considered rather than followed blindly. For example, if you're testing on multiple devices or with different user types, then you need to apply this rule to all of those segments. You may also want to add 1-2 additional "buffer" sessions to account for poorer quality participants, tech issues, no shows, etc.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Userlytics](https://www.userlytics.com)

- [Usertesting.com](https://www.usertesting.com)

- [Maze](https://maze.co)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Engagement Decay & Habit Research](/research-recipes/engagement-decay)

- [Involuntary Churn & Payment Recovery Research](/research-recipes/involuntary-churn)

- [Researching With Low Traffic](/research-recipes/researching-low-traffic)

- [Validating a Redesign Before Build](/research-recipes/validating-redesign)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/prototype-testing
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Remote Usability Studies

Use a sample pool of participants who match your target audience. Watch and listen as they walk through your site and perform tasks set by you, designed to emulate your core user journey or area of focus. Tasks and questions are set up within an external tool, meaning participants complete the session independently in their own time, thinking out loud as they go. Once complete, the recording of their screen, voice over (and sometimes webcam image) will be accessible within the tool for analysis.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore, Focus, Validate |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | Medium |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Any surface |

## When to reach for it

Gather insight into on-site friction points on a specific page, piece of functionality, core user journey, or full website. Uncovers key areas of confusion, frustration, and barriers to conversion. Gather data on metrics such as task success rate, time per task, System Usability Score, etc.

## Strengths

One of the key benefits of remote usability studies vs. moderated is that it is conducted from the comfort of the participant's own home, using their own devices. This helps make the session more realistic. The fact there is no moderator or live observers can also help prevent research bias such as the Hawthorne effect.

## Limits

The remote nature of the sessions means that users can sometimes go "off track" or misunderstand the tasks, which can negatively impact or invalidate the insights and data. The lack of a moderator means there's no limited control over the session, including bringing the participant back on track or gathering more specific insights by asking specific and / or follow up questions.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Tool
There are many remote usability study tools, with slightly different capabilities and pricing models. Much like with AB testing tools, the success of your research is not necessarily determined by the tool you use, but by what you do with it (e.g. accurate recruitment, well-crafted tasks, and questions, etc). Key considerations when picking a tool include; the size and quality of their participant panel, the ability to add a recruitment screener, the analysis capabilities, what's included (e.g. participant incentives). Also double check how their pricing works, e.g. does it scale up based on the recruitment criteria and estimated length of session.

### Sample Size
Nielsen Norman says "The answer is 5, except when it's not" regarding usability study sample size. We use this as a guide; but one that should be considered rather than followed blindly. For example, if you're testing on multiple devices or with different user types, then you need to apply this rule to all of those segments. You may also want to add 1-2 additional "buffer" sessions to account for poorer quality participants, tech issues, no shows, etc.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Userlytics](https://www.userlytics.com)

- [Usertesting.com](https://www.usertesting.com)

- [Askable](https://askable.com)

- [UserZoom](https://www.usertesting.com)

- [Lookback](https://www.lookback.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [B2B ICP Research](/research-recipes/b2b-icp-research)

- [Category & Listing Page Optimisation](/research-recipes/category-listing-page)

- [Checkout & Cart Optimisation](/research-recipes/checkout-cart-optimisation)

- [Conversion Research](/research-recipes/conversion-research)

- [Lead-Gen Form Optimisation](/research-recipes/lead-gen-form)

- [Mobile Experience Optimisation](/research-recipes/mobile-experience)

- [Navigation & Information Architecture](/research-recipes/navigation-information-architecture)

- [Onboarding & Activation Research](/research-recipes/onboarding-activation)

# Sales / Customer Service Interviews

Sales / Customer Support interviews involve running 30 minute to 1 hour sessions with members of the sales team and/or the customer service team, either in person or remotely on Zoom, Teams, etc. Team members are recruited via email, either directly or through a client point of contact. These interviews draw on the internal teams who interact with customers every day, uncovering customer motivations, FUDs and frictions. This tribal knowledge from sales and customer service can then be applied to improve the website.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | Low |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Messaging & copy, Pricing page |

## When to reach for it

Sales / Customer Support interviews are an effective method when running exploratory research.
Sales interviews can be particularly useful when looking to develop or enhance ideal customer profiles, or personas. Speaking to sales teams can help you understand customers (and potential customers) key triggers and motivations for seeking out your product or service. You can also use sales interviews to uncover the primary barriers to conversion; the reasons why potential customers don't convert.
Customer support/service interviews are effective when looking to understand customer's key issues or frustrations. This type of data can be useful when focusing on retention for subscription products/services. This activity can also identify key questions that users have that could be answered on the website.

## Strengths

Interviews allow you to dig deeper than surveys by asking follow-up questions based on answers. This makes them more appropriate for more complex use cases or when you have a more specific area of focus.
Running interviews with Sales / Customer Support teams provides you with a snapshot of the top customer problems from an internal perspective.

## Limits

There could be some bias in this data, given that it is internal data (and could be a negative reflection on internal teams).
This data about what is important to customers, or customer pain points is being filtered, e.g. it is not coming directly from the customer.
Running interviews can be time-consuming, which means they are not effective for gathering large samples of data (unless you have a large budget / a lot of time resources). To help mitigate this, interviews can be used alongside a survey to gather both in-depth, high quality insights at a large scale.
An insightful interview is determined by the questions you ask. Much like running moderated usability studies, there is skill involved inrunning an effective interview. You need to avoid leading questions, and also ensure questions are not multifaceted as this can cause difficulty in analysis.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Logistics
If you're planning and running the sessions yourself, there are a few logistics to keep in mind;

- Booking a timeslot; before you send the initial email asking for people to take part, consider how you'll organise the sessions. You could share a Calendly link or something similar to allow participant's to book directly you. Whatever you use, you want to avoid having to manually agree on a date / time by going back and forth via email.

- Tool; you can use any video conferencing tool (Zoom, Teams, Hangouts, etc). Don't forget to record the sessions (but ask permission first) to ensure you don't have to write everything down when you're running the interview.

- No shows; when interviews internal participants, the chance of a no-show is relatively low. However, consider how to mitigate this, for example, sending out a series of reminders in the days / hours running up to the session, as well as over recruiting (e.g. running 1-2 more sessions than you need). Mention in your comms that you will wait for 10 minutes before assuming a no-show, so you don't have to sit and wait for the full amount of time until they turn up.

### Sample Size
The goal of this activity is to gather qualitative insights, therefore the sample size doesn't need to be high. Use a similar theory to with usability studies; Nielsen Norman says "The answer is 5, except when it's not" regarding usability study sample size. We use this as a guide; but one that should be considered rather than followed blindly. You also need to consider the size of the organisation and if this is a representative sample.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Zoom](https://zoom.us)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Brand Perception Baseline & Tracking](/research-recipes/brand-perception-tracking)

- [Lead Quality Research](/research-recipes/lead-quality)

- [SaaS Pricing Page](/research-recipes/saas-pricing-page)

- [Traffic Quality & Channel Fit Research](/research-recipes/traffic-quality-channel-fit)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/sales-customer-service-interviews
Last updated: 2026-08-06

# Sales / Customer Service Survey

A survey sent by email to members of the sales team and/or the customer service team. These surveys gather insight from the internal teams who interact with customers every day, uncovering customer motivations, FUDs and frictions. This tribal knowledge from sales and customer service can then be applied to improve the website.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | Low |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Messaging & copy, Pricing page |

## When to reach for it

Sales / Customer Support surveys are an effective method when running exploratory research.
Sales / Customer Support surveys can be particularly useful when looking to develop or enhance ideal customer profiles, or personas. Speaking to sales teams can help you understand customers (and potential customers) key triggers and motivations for seeking out your product or service. You can also use sales interviews to uncover the primary barriers to conversion; the reasons why potential customers don't convert.
Customer support/service surveys are effective when looking to understand customer's key issues or frustrations. This type of data can be useful when focusing on retention for subscription products/services. This activity can also identify key questions that users have that could be answered on the website.

## Strengths

A customer survey allows you to gather large samples of data, which isn't possible when running customer interviews. Customer surveys can also be used alongside customer interviews to increase the depth of insight.
Customer surveys allow you to gather both qualitative and quantitative data, depending on the types of questions you ask.

## Limits

An insightful customer survey is determined by the questions you ask. you need to avoid leading questions, and also ensure questions are not multifaceted as this can cause difficulty in analysis.
There could be some bias in this data, given that it is internal data (and could be a negative reflection on internal teams).
This data about what is important to customers, or customer pain points is being filtered, e.g. it is not coming directly from the customer.
It can be a challenge to code and analyse large sets of qualitative data.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Tool
The survey could be built in a range of tools, including Google Forms, TypeForm, Survey Monkey, etc. There are plenty of free tools available for this activity, so there's not really any need to pay for a tool, unless you have more bespoke needs, e.g. large data sets, custom question logic, etc.

### Sample Size
The goal of this activity is to gather quantitative insights, therefore the sample size should be relatively high. However, it is unlikely you will achieve a similar sample size to a customer survey (approx 300 responses) depending on the size of the organisation and number of employees in the sales / customer survey teams. As such, you should aim for gathering the biggest sample possible, given the size of the teams.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Google Forms](https://www.google.com/forms/about/)

- [Survey Monkey](https://www.surveymonkey.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Lead Quality Research](/research-recipes/lead-quality)

- [Repeat Purchase & Post-Purchase Research](/research-recipes/repeat-purchase)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/sales-customer-service-survey
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Search & SERP Analysis

Analysis of organic search performance and the surrounding results landscape. The queries that bring visitors in and the ones that should but don't, rankings and click-through against the pages that hold them, and the content competitors use to win the intents that matter. Pairs the site's search data with the language customers actually type. Branded query volume belongs here too, since demand for the brand by name, tracked over time, is one of the few behavioural reads on brand awareness.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore, Focus |
| Data type | Quantitative |
| Strength of signal | High |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Acquisition & ads, Landing pages |

## When to reach for it

Grow qualified organic traffic, close the gap between customer search language and site language, prioritise content investment by intent, and connect organic acquisition to on-site optimisation. Track branded search demand as a behavioural indicator of brand awareness, before and after brand-level changes.

## Strengths

Real behavioural data at scale from actual customer queries. Shows demand and competitive position without spending on a panel or media.

## Limits

Intent has to be inferred from queries rather than asked. Rankings move slowly, so validating changes takes time and can be confounded by algorithm updates.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Google Search Console](https://search.google.com/search-console/about)

- [Ahrefs](https://ahrefs.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Brand Perception Baseline & Tracking](/research-recipes/brand-perception-tracking)

- [SEO & Search Intent Research](/research-recipes/seo-search-intent)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/search-serp-analysis
Last updated: 2026-08-06

# Session Recordings

Session recording analysis involves watching recordings of real users interacting with the website, using a tool added into your website code. Recordings show the pages users view, where they scroll and click, and their mouse movements. It's also possible to see things like "rage clicks" where a user clicks on something multiple times in frustration.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore, Focus, Validate |
| Data type | Quantitative |
| Strength of signal | Low |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Any surface |

## When to reach for it

Session recordings can provide you with insight into real user's on-site behaviour which can help you identify areas of friction, frustration or barriers to conversion.
Observing session recordings can be beneficial for gathering an overall understanding of how users are interacting with your website, as well as digging into interactions with specific pages or elements.
Session recordings can also be used to watch users interacting with any live experiments. This can be beneficial from a QA and an analysis perspective.

## Strengths

Observe real user behaviour with no research bias; users don't specifically know they are being recorded.
Helps bring other data such as digital analytics numbers "to life", by providing a more visual representation of the data. For example, Analytics might show a high exit rate from the basket page, session recordings can help explain why this is happening by showing users interacting with the basket (and potentially experiencing issues).

## Limits

Session recordings are open to interpretation, since there's a lack of explanation of the behaviour. You may see someone doing something, but you won't necessarily know why they are doing that (and you can't ask them).
Session recording analysis can be time-consuming, since you have to manually watch the recordings. There are ways to reduce this, such as speeding up recordings, skipping periods of inactivity and using filters to ensure you only watch the recordings that are most relevant to your research needs.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Analysis & Interpretation
The primary consideration with session recording analysis is how to approach the analysis part. Typically one person within a team would watch either a set number of recordings or spend a set amount of time watching recordings. Although multiple people could also conduct this activity, perhaps focusing on different pages, elements or user type. It is important to establish a strategy for tagging and note-taking that is used consistently to support analysis and prevent insights from getting lost or diluted.
For example, say you're watching 100 recordings. You might see some behaviours in the first 5 recordings that don't appear to be particularly interesting, but after 80 recordings you see that this behaviour actually happened in the large majority of sessions you've watched. This is why it is important to tag all behaviours from the beginning (within reason).
It can be beneficial to gather multiple people together for analysis and interpretation of behaviours. Once you've watched and tagged multiple recordings, get together with your team to share what you found and hypothesise about why this behaviour might be happening. Since there is no way of knowing the truth at this stage, it can help to have multiple points of view.

### Qualitative vs. Quantitative
Although strictly speaking, session recordings are a form of digital analytics and therefore quantitative in nature, given the time involved in watching individual sessions in order to truly pull quantitative data from this method, you can think of session recordings as qualitative and heatmaps as their quantitative counterpart. In a similar way to surveys being useful for gathering large quantities of data, and interviews being effective for gathering a smaller, but higher quality of insight.

### Tools
Tools include Hotjar, Content Square, Full Story and Microsoft Clarity. These tools have a very wide range of price points, typically Hotjar was the tool of choice due to it's reasonable price point, but this has increased in price more recently. Microsoft Clarity offers a free solution.

# Social Media Listening

Systematic monitoring of what people say about a brand, its competitors and its category across social platforms, forums and communities. It captures the unprompted voice of the market: the words people use, the complaints and praise they volunteer, and how the conversation shifts over time.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore |
| Data type | Qualitative / Quantitative |
| Strength of signal | Low |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Any surface, Messaging & copy |

## When to reach for it

Hear how the market talks about the brand and its competitors when nobody is asking.Surface the vocabulary customers use for the category, to feed messaging and search work.Watch how conversation volume and sentiment shift around a launch, rebrand or incident.Find where the audience actually gathers, which for technical audiences is often forums and communities rather than mainstream platforms.

## Strengths

Unprompted and continuous, so there is no interviewer effect and no survey fatigue.
Covers competitors as easily as the brand itself.
Picks up shifts quickly, where structured research only catches them at the next wave.

## Limits

The people who post are not a representative sample of the market, and loud voices skew the read.
Volume can be thin for niche and B2B categories, so weeks can pass without meaningful signal.
Sentiment classification is rough. Irony, jargon and mixed opinions get mislabelled.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Where to listen
The right sources depend on the audience. Developer and technical audiences live in forums, communities and Q&A sites more than mainstream social platforms, so pick sources by where the buyers actually talk, not by what the tool covers best.

### Baseline before judging
Raw mention counts mean little on their own. Track against a baseline period and against competitors so a change reads as signal rather than noise.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Brandwatch](https://www.brandwatch.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Brand Perception Baseline & Tracking](/research-recipes/brand-perception-tracking)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/social-media-listening
Last updated: 2026-08-06

# Tree Testing

Tree testing involves replicating a website navigation (existing or proposed) in a link "tree". Recruited participants are then set tasks to find specific content or information within the link tree. This provides data on how easy specific content is to find within the navigational structure.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Focus, Validate |
| Data type | Quantitative |
| Strength of signal | Medium |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Navigation & IA |

## When to reach for it

Tree testing is similar to card sorting in that it provides insight into the navigational structure of a website.
It can be used to gather initial data into where the main issues are within an existing navigational structure (as identified via other research methods), and it can also be used as a validation technique to validate changes/improvements.

## Strengths

Tree testing is a relatively unique research method due to its focused nature (specifically focused on website content structure).
Tree testing provides insight into how easy content is to find within an existing or proposed navigational structure.
Tree testing can be done on existing structures to identify issues and opportunities or on proposed structures to validate changes.
Tools like OptimalWorkshop make tree testing relatively quick and easy to set up and run.

## Limits

Data analysis can be difficult/time intensive. The data provided by tools like OptimalWorkshop is extensive and although can be very insightful, it takes some understanding of the data to accurately interpret it.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Sample Size
Tree testing is primarily a quantitative method, and as such the sample size should be treated accordingly. There isn't a one-size-fits all number; instead the right number is based on the level of precision needed. Most tree tests have between 50-150 participants.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Userlytics](https://www.userlytics.com)

- [Optimal Workshop](https://www.optimalworkshop.com)

- [UserZoom](https://www.usertesting.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Navigation & Information Architecture](/research-recipes/navigation-information-architecture)

## Go deeper

Go deeper

- [Tree testing, fast iterative evaluation of menu labels (NN/g)](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/tree-testing/)

- [Card sorting vs tree testing (NN/g)](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-tree-testing-differences/)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/tree-testing

# UX Heuristic Review

A UX heuristic review in this context is a review of a website based on a set of guiding UX principles, with the aim to identify areas of potential UX friction (ultimately areas of the user experience that could be creating friction or barriers for users on that website). A UX Heuristic review can be conducted on any digital experience; from a full website or core user journey, through to a single page, a piece of functionality, or a design or prototype.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore, Focus |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | Low |
| Effort | Low |
| Surface area | Any surface |

## When to reach for it

A UX heuristic review is a good starting point for an experimentation programme or larger research project. This is a particularly effective option in the case of low traffic pages which making it difficult to run polls or analyze analytics data. A UX heuristic review can also be used when there's limited time / budget to run alternative user research activities.

## Strengths

A good starting point, particularly if you’re not very familiar with the website, e.g. you’re new to a business or working in an agency.
It’s relatively quick and inexpensive (no tool costs, only resource costs).
Can be used as an effective tool for encouraging collaboration across teams, and for helping build a culture of experimentation.
Identifies “low hanging fruit” such as bugs and JDIs.

## Limits

Low strength of signal; insights aren’t based on real user data (therefore should not be used to validate high-risk business decisions).
Can be misused to push personal agendas, personal opinions, etc.
Additional research is (ideally) needed to support/validate insights.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations
There are two steps involved in conducting a robust heuristic review; a group workshop and a scoring exercise conducted by a smaller team.
The group workshop is a great way to gather insights from a wide range of people in a short period of time. This is an effective way to help avoid personal opinion; as the workshop will focus on identifying the themes that come up across individuals and groups.
We recommend running the workshop with up to 10 people for between 1 hour and 1 hour 30 minutes. Assuming the workshop is being run remotely, you can use a tool like Miro or FigJam to run the workshop, if you're running it in person, you can use post-it notes instead.
Example agenda;- Background & Intro - 10 mins- Group breakout sessions:Part 1 (solo review, note taking & classification) 20 minsPart 2 (discuss & agree top 3) 10 mins- Each group present back top 3-5 / group discussion - 20 mins
Next, is the scoring matrix. This is where a smaller project team dig further into the detail. This can also help validate what was discovered in the workshop. This involves up to 5 people scoring the user experience in a spreadsheet against a set of UX guidelines (see example in Resources).

## Common tools

Tools

- [Miro](https://miro.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [Acquisition Research](/research-recipes/acquisition-research)

- [Conversion Research](/research-recipes/conversion-research)

- [Landing Page Optimisation](/research-recipes/landing-page-optimisation)

- [Researching With Low Traffic](/research-recipes/researching-low-traffic)

- [SaaS Pricing Page](/research-recipes/saas-pricing-page)

- [Trust & Credibility Audit](/research-recipes/trust-credibility)

## Go deeper

Go deeper

- [ResearchXL model](https://speero.com/post/how-to-create-winning-tests-using-the-researchxl-model)

- [ResearchXL blueprint](https://speero.com/blueprints/research-xl)

- [Example review, Lily's Kitchen](https://speero.com/post/a-heuristic-review-of-lilys-kitchen)

- [Example review, WHOOP](https://speero.com/post/an-heuristic-review-of-whoop-com)

# Win-loss Analysis (CRM Analysis)

Analysis of data housed within existing CRM (Customer Relationship Management) tool / database, e.g. Salesforce, Pipedrive, etc. to understand customers and potential customers challenges, pain points, blockers, decision making process, etc. on a large scale and identify nuances between different customer types.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore |
| Data type | Quantitative |
| Strength of signal | Medium |
| Effort | Medium |
| Surface area | Messaging & copy, Pricing page |

## When to reach for it

Lack insight into ICPs specific motivations, pain points, FUDs.Struggling to convert leads into paid customers.Messaging and content is informed by internal assumptions, opinions, etc. rather than data and insight.Have difficulty effectively communicating the value proposition, what problems you solve for businesses, etc.Need to build ICPs and personas from scratch to help inform wider marketing efforts.

## Strengths

No need to conduct new research / collect data & insights.
Gather insights from real users who have a genuine need for your product or service.
Understand the key questions and barriers holding users back from converting.

## Limits

Can be difficult to conduct effectively if CRM data is not well organised, record is not kept of sales conversations, reasons for not converting, etc.
May be subject to some bias if based solely on notes from sales team within CRM.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Sample Size
In this case sample size will depend on the amount of data you have, which will relate to the number of leads, prospects, customers, etc. It will also depend on the depth of the data. If you only have top level data, then aim for more (200-300), whereas if you have detailed, more qualitative data, then you could aim lower 50-100 responses. Also consider the different segments within your sample if you're including convertors and those who did not convert, you need an appropriate sample size for both / all segments.

## Common tools

Tools
Runs on your existing systems; no dedicated tool required.

## Recipes that use this method

- [B2B ICP Research](/research-recipes/b2b-icp-research)

- [Churn & Retention Research](/research-recipes/churn-retention)

- [Free Trial to Paid Conversion](/research-recipes/trial-to-paid)

- [Involuntary Churn & Payment Recovery Research](/research-recipes/involuntary-churn)

- [Lead Quality Research](/research-recipes/lead-quality)

- [Traffic Quality & Channel Fit Research](/research-recipes/traffic-quality-channel-fit)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/win-loss-analysis
Last updated: 2026-07-20

# Win-loss Interviews

One-to-one interviews with recent buyers and lost prospects about how the purchase decision actually went: the trigger that started the search, the alternatives weighed, the objections that nearly killed the deal, and what tipped it in the end. Run like customer interviews, but the sample deliberately includes the deals you lost, which is where the sharpest positioning insight lives.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stage | Explore, Focus |
| Data type | Qualitative |
| Strength of signal | Medium |
| Effort | High |
| Surface area | Messaging & copy, Pricing page |

## When to reach for it

Understand why deals are won and lost in the buyer's own words. Feeds ICP research, positioning and messaging with the market's real decision criteria and vocabulary, and locates the funnel stages where deals stall or die. Adds the why behind the patterns CRM win-loss analysis surfaces.

## Strengths

Covers the buyers you lost, whose reasons never surface in customer research. First-hand accounts of the decision replace the sales team's secondhand recollection, and the buyer's own language feeds straight into positioning and messaging work.

## Limits

Lost prospects are harder to recruit and often need a neutral interviewer plus a real incentive to speak candidly. Samples stay small, so the findings show the shape of the decision rather than its frequency.

## Practical considerations

Practical considerations

### Recruitment
Reach out within a few weeks of the decision, while the detail is still fresh. Lost prospects speak more honestly to a neutral third party than to anyone from the vendor, so consider who conducts the sessions. A meaningful incentive matters more here than in customer research, since lost prospects owe you nothing.

### Sample size
Qualitative goals apply: a handful of wins and a handful of losses per segment is a workable guide, and the losses are usually where the sharpest insight sits. Pair with CRM win-loss analysis when the pattern needs scale behind it.

## Common tools

Tools

- [Zoom](https://zoom.us)

- [Lookback](https://www.lookback.com)

## Recipes that use this method

- [B2B ICP Research](/research-recipes/b2b-icp-research)

- [Lead Quality Research](/research-recipes/lead-quality)

Source: https://speero.com/research-methods/win-loss-interviews
Last updated: 2026-07-20
